quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of a simple dyed-fabric costing for export.

questions.q: Why are commission and the export surcharge divided out of the proceeds rather than added to cost?
options: They are paid in US dollars
They are percentages of the selling proceeds, not of cost
They are fixed amounts per container
They are recovered from the buyer separately
questions.explain: Commission and EDS are charged as a percentage of what the exporter receives, so the required proceeds must be divided by (1 − commission − EDS). Adding the percentage to cost would understate the price slightly.

questions.q: The gross grey price per finished metre is the local grey price divided by (1 − wastage and shrinkage).
questions.explain: Processing loses part of every grey metre, so more than one grey metre is bought for each finished metre: Rs 100 ÷ (1 − 0.10) = Rs 111.11.

questions.q: In the lecture sheet, how much B-grade fabric is assumed to be available for sale?
options: None; wastage is a total loss
questions.explain: The sheet takes B-grade available as half of the wastage: 10% wastage gives 5% B-grade. The other half is genuinely lost in shrinkage and cutting.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation EDS stand for in a Pakistani export costing?
questions.explain: EDS is the Export Development Surcharge, a small percentage (0.25% in the sheet) deducted from export proceeds. It is not a dyeing charge and not a duty refund.

questions.q: In this sheet the margin is calculated as a percentage of total cost, not of the selling price.
questions.explain: Line 20 is a margin on cost: proceeds required = total cost × (1 + margin). A margin on sales price would need a division, like the commission.

questions.q: Which group of costs is first worked out per container and then divided by the metres in the container?
options: Dyeing charges and local transport to the dyer
Grey fabric price and B-grade credit
Inland transport, freight, forwarding and bank charges
questions.explain: The variable export costs (Rs 15,000 transport, US$ 500 freight, Rs 3,500 forwarding, US$ 200 and Rs 3,000 bank charges) are per 40 ft container and are spread over 107,745 m. Dyeing is already per metre.

questions.q: The line "B-grade proceeds (credit)" shows (2.22). What does the credit do to the costing?
options: It is added to the dyeing charge
It reduces the cost per finished metre
It is a penalty paid to the buyer
It is the price of the B-grade fabric per metre
questions.explain: The B-grade fabric is sold locally at 40% of the grey price; its proceeds come off the cost of the A-grade metre, so the figure is shown in brackets as a deduction.

questions.q: The required price is converted from US$ per metre to US$ per yard. Which factor is used?
questions.explain: There are 1.0936 yards in a metre, so a yard is shorter and cheaper: price per yard = price per metre ÷ 1.0936. Multiplying would give a higher, wrong price.

questions.q: The US$ 500 freight must be converted at the exchange rate before it can be added to the rupee costs per metre.
questions.explain: The sheet works in rupees until the last two lines: freight US$ 500 × Rs 60 = Rs 30,000 per container, then ÷ 107,745 m = Rs 0.278 per metre.

questions.q: The heading "Variable export cost per metre (less EDS & commission)" means that EDS and commission are:
options: Already included in the five lines below it
Excluded here and applied later as a percentage of proceeds
Paid by the buyer, so ignored
Fixed costs of the export office
questions.explain: The five per-container items are amounts in rupees or dollars; EDS and commission depend on the final price, so they are handled afterwards on line 22 by dividing the proceeds.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which formula, which direction: how each input in the dyed-fabric sheet moves the quotation.

questions.q: Grey price G and wastage w. Which formula gives the gross grey price per finished metre?
questions.explain: If w is lost, only (1 − w) of each grey metre becomes finished fabric, so each finished metre costs G ÷ (1 − w). G × (1 + w) is the common mistake and gives Rs 110 instead of Rs 111.11.

questions.q: Grey price stays at Rs 100 but wastage and shrinkage rise from 10% to 20%. The gross grey price per finished metre becomes:
questions.explain: Rs 100 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = Rs 125. Rs 120 is the result of wrongly adding 20%.

questions.q: With proceeds required P, commission c and EDS e, the proceeds including commission and EDS are:
questions.explain: The exporter must receive P after c and e are deducted from the invoice, so invoice × (1 − c − e) = P, giving invoice = P ÷ (1 − c − e).

questions.q: Adding 1.25% to Rs 157.06 instead of dividing by 0.9875 gives a slightly lower required price.
questions.explain: 157.06 × 1.0125 = Rs 159.02 against 157.06 ÷ 0.9875 = Rs 159.05. The difference is small here but grows with higher commission rates.

questions.q: If the same container can be packed with more metres, the export cost per metre:
options: Falls, because the per-container charges are spread over more metres
Falls only for the freight line
questions.explain: All five export items are fixed per container; dividing them by a larger metreage lowers every one of them, not just freight.

questions.q: The rupee proceeds per metre are turned into a US$ price per metre by:
questions.explain: Rs 159.05 per metre ÷ Rs 60 per US$ = US$ 2.6508 per metre. Dividing by 1.0936 is the yard conversion, a later step.

questions.q: The exchange rate rises from Rs 60 to Rs 70 per US$ while all rupee costs stay the same. The required US$ price per metre:
questions.explain: Almost all cost is in rupees, so dividing by a larger rate gives fewer dollars. The dollar freight and bank items rise in rupees, but by only a few paisa per metre.

questions.q: B-grade credit per finished metre = grey price × B-grade fraction × B-grade price fraction ÷ (1 − wastage).
questions.explain: The sheet formula is C1 × B4 × B5 ÷ (1 − B2): Rs 100 × 0.05 × 0.40 ÷ 0.90 = Rs 2.22, because the B-grade arises per grey metre and must be expressed per finished metre.

questions.q: For the same fabric, the required price per yard compared with the price per metre is:
options: Lower only if the exchange rate is above 60
questions.explain: A yard (0.9144 m) is shorter than a metre, so it carries less cost: US$ 2.6508 per metre ÷ 1.0936 = US$ 2.4239 per yard.

questions.q: To which line is the 5% margin applied in the sheet?
options: The total processing cost before export costs
The total cost per metre including export cost
The proceeds after commission and EDS
questions.explain: Line 21 = line 19 × 1.05, and line 19 is total processing cost plus export cost per metre. Margin is taken on the full cost, before commission and EDS are divided out.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Rebuild the lecture's dyed-fabric sheet line by line, from grey price to the dollar quotation.

questions.q: Local grey price Rs 100 per metre, wastage and shrinkage 10%. What is the gross grey price per finished metre (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: Rs 100 ÷ 0.90 = Rs 111.11 per finished metre.

questions.q: A different grey fabric costs Rs 120 per metre and the dyer reports 8% wastage and shrinkage. Gross grey price per finished metre, to the nearest paisa?
Grey price Rs 100, wastage 10%, B-grade available is half the wastage and sells at 40% of the grey price. What is the B-grade credit per finished metre (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: B-grade fraction = 10% ÷ 2 = 5%; credit = 100 × 0.05 × 0.40 ÷ 0.90 = Rs 2.22 per finished metre.

questions.q: Inland transport is Rs 15,000 per 40 ft container holding 107,745 m. Transport cost per metre, to three decimals?
Freight is US$ 500 per container at Rs 60 per US$; the container holds 107,745 m. Freight per metre, to three decimals?
questions.explain: 500 × 60 = Rs 30,000 per container; ÷ 107,745 = Rs 0.278 per metre.

questions.q: Per container: transport Rs 15,000, freight US$ 500, forwarding Rs 3,500, foreign bank US$ 200, local bank Rs 3,000; exchange rate Rs 60; 107,745 m per container. Total export cost per metre, to three decimals?
Total cost is Rs 149.58 per metre and the exporter wants a 5% margin on cost. Proceeds required per metre, to the nearest paisa?
Proceeds required are Rs 157.06 per metre; commission is 1% and EDS 0.25% of proceeds. What invoice proceeds per metre are needed (to the nearest paisa)?
Rs 159.05 per metre at Rs 60 per US$ is a required price of:
questions.explain: 159.05 ÷ 60 = US$ 2.65 per metre. US$ 2.42 is the price per yard; 0.38 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

questions.q: A price of US$ 2.6508 per metre expressed per yard is:
questions.explain: 2.6508 ÷ 1.0936 = US$ 2.42 per yard. US$ 2.90 is the result of multiplying by 1.0936 instead of dividing.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions in the export costing office: which dyer, which container load, and what goes wrong when a formula is misapplied.

questions.q: Of the following, which action reduces the export cost per metre the most?
options: Loading more metres into each 40 ft container
Selling the B-grade at a higher price
questions.explain: Export cost per metre is per-container charges ÷ metres per container, so only the container load changes it. Dyeing charge and B-grade price affect processing cost, not export cost.

questions.q: Dyer A charges Rs 40 per metre with 15% wastage; dyer B charges Rs 42 with 10% wastage. Grey price is Rs 100, B-grade is half the wastage at 40% of grey, local transport Rs 0.10 either way. Which is cheaper per finished metre?
Because commission is charged on proceeds, quoting a higher price also raises the commission paid in rupees.
questions.explain: 1% of a bigger invoice is a bigger rupee amount; that is why the sheet divides by (1 − c − e) rather than adding a fixed sum.

questions.q: A clerk adds 1.25% to the proceeds required instead of dividing by 0.9875. The effect on the quotation is that it:
questions.explain: Multiplying by 1.0125 gives Rs 159.02 instead of Rs 159.05, so the exporter will receive a few paisa per metre less than the planned margin.

questions.q: The price is fixed at US$ 2.6508 per metre and then the exchange rate moves from Rs 60 to Rs 65 before shipment. With rupee costs unchanged, the exporter:
options: Receives fewer rupees and loses margin
Receives more rupees per metre, so profit rises
Is unaffected because the price is in dollars
Must requote at a lower dollar price
questions.explain: 2.6508 × 65 = Rs 172.30 per metre against Rs 159.05 planned; the rupee costs are unchanged so the extra is profit (less the small rise in dollar freight and bank charges).

questions.q: The B-grade market weakens and B-grade now fetches only 20% of the grey price instead of 40%. The effect on cost per finished metre is:
options: No change, because B-grade is wastage
questions.explain: The credit halves from Rs 2.22 to Rs 1.11 (100 × 0.05 × 0.20 ÷ 0.90), so cost rises by Rs 1.11 per metre.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of the variable export cost in the lecture sheet?
questions.explain: Office rent is a fixed cost of the business, recovered through the margin; the sheet's export cost holds only the per-container items that vary with shipments.

questions.q: B-grade fabric sold locally at only 40% of the grey price still lowers the cost of each A-grade metre.
questions.explain: Any proceeds from fabric that would otherwise be a loss are credited against the cost of good fabric; the sheet shows Rs 2.22 per metre.

questions.q: A buyer asks for the price per yard. The clerk divides the US$ 2.6508 per metre by 0.9144 instead of 1.0936. The quotation is:
questions.explain: 2.6508 ÷ 0.9144 = US$ 2.90, 20% above the right US$ 2.42. Dividing by metres-per-yard is the wrong way round; the buyer will reject the price.

questions.q: A buyer orders only 50,000 m but the shipment still carries the same Rs 63,500 of per-container charges. Export cost per metre becomes:
questions.explain: 63,500 ÷ 50,000 = Rs 1.27 per metre, more than double the Rs 0.589 on a full 107,745 m container. Small shipments need their own export cost line.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder, two-step questions across the whole dyed-fabric costing, including working backwards from a target price.

questions.q: Grey Rs 110 per metre, wastage 12%, B-grade available half the wastage sold at 35% of grey, dyeing Rs 45, local transport Rs 0.10. Total processing cost per finished metre, to the nearest paisa?
Total cost is Rs 149.58 per metre. Margin on cost 8%, commission 2%, EDS 0.25%. Invoice proceeds required per metre, to the nearest paisa?
Which two export items rise in rupees when the rupee weakens against the dollar?
questions.explain: Freight (US$ 500) and the foreign bank charge (US$ 200) are in dollars and are multiplied by the exchange rate; the other items are already in rupees.

questions.q: Halving wastage from 10% to 5% reduces the gross grey price per finished metre by exactly Rs 5.56.
questions.explain: 100 ÷ 0.95 = Rs 105.26 against Rs 111.11, a fall of Rs 5.85, not half of the Rs 11.11 gross-up. The relationship is not linear because of the division by (1 − w).

questions.q: A buyer will pay at most US$ 2.50 per metre. Exchange rate Rs 60, commission 1%, EDS 0.25%, margin on cost 5%. What is the maximum total cost per metre the exporter can afford (to the nearest paisa)?
questions.explain: Rupee proceeds = 2.50 × 60 = 150; net of commission and EDS = 150 × 0.9875 = 148.13; remove the 5% margin: 148.13 ÷ 1.05 = Rs 141.07.

questions.q: Which of these errors produces a required price that is too LOW?
options: Dividing the grey price by (1 + wastage) instead of (1 − wastage)
Adding commission to cost and also dividing it out of proceeds
Using the price per metre when the buyer asked per yard
questions.explain: 100 ÷ 1.10 = Rs 90.91 instead of Rs 111.11, so the whole costing starts Rs 20 too low. The other three errors all push the price up.

questions.q: A dyer quotes dyeing at Rs 36.58 per yard. Converted to per metre this is:
questions.explain: A metre is 1.0936 yards, so 36.58 × 1.0936 = Rs 40.00 per metre. Dividing by 1.0936 (Rs 33.45) would understate the charge.

questions.q: Per-container export charges total Rs 63,500. How many metres would a container need to hold for export cost to fall to Rs 0.50 per metre?
questions.explain: 63,500 ÷ 0.50 = 127,000 m, about 18% more than the 107,745 m in the lecture.

questions.q: The price is fixed at US$ 2.65 per metre and the exchange rate later becomes Rs 66. After 1% commission and 0.25% EDS the exporter nets, per metre:
questions.explain: 2.65 × 66 = Rs 174.90 invoice; × 0.9875 = Rs 172.71 net. Rs 174.90 forgets the deductions; Rs 159.05 is the original plan at Rs 60.

questions.q: For the same fabric and quotation, the required price per yard is always lower than the required price per metre.
questions.explain: A yard is 0.9144 of a metre and carries proportionally less cost, so the per-yard figure is the per-metre figure ÷ 1.0936.
